comparator.name: Bachelor Geneeskunde
comparator.sourceNotes: Current 2026–2027 Erasmusarts 2030 OER and appendices govern this full-time Dutch-taught 180-EC Bachelor Geneeskunde (CROHO 56551). Partial English teaching supports the literature; the normalized target is not an English or part-time route. No formal specialist bachelor track is selected; the ordinary programme is retained, not the separate individually approved vrij onderwijsprogramma. Appendix 2 articles 9–10 and table 2 define 13 integrated case-based blocks, four projects and five longitudinal lines: clinical skills, identity/professionalism, social engagement, academic formation and technology. Workload is evenly spread across three years; the five display components retain 60 EC of Year-1 workload, 60 EC of Year-2 workload, 30 EC minor, 29 EC of final integrated study and the separately specified 1 EC of longitudinal professionalism. These are workload/coverage accounting groups, not official separately credited year courses: only 30 EC is awarded at the first-year progression decision, 30 EC after the minor, and the remaining credits at the final examination to reach 180. The 1 EC of professionalism is included, not added to 180; its final-year placement is an accounting convention because it is awarded at the examination. No EC is invented for individual themes, projects, competencies or assessments. The clinical skills and professional lines are compulsory integrated teaching. Year 3 includes competency-linked final works within its integrated blocks; the Medical Science project is not a separately credited thesis. OER article 4.4 requires 30 EC of broadening minor study: an eligible 30-EC minor or at least 15 EC plus another minor or approved university electives; external institutions outside the named EUR/TU Delft/Leiden group and all elective packages require prior Examination Board permission. OER article 4.1 and appendices 3–6 govern progression: a favourable decision and 30-EC BSA at the end of Ba1, another favourable decision before the minor, and a further decision before Block 11. These involve block-test and competency standards, professional conduct and iVTG participation/POP reflections, rather than ordinary 60-EC yearly completion thresholds. Final requirements include all block tests attempted, none below level, all competencies at level, iVTG level 12 in Ba3, completed BLS2 and no active remediation process. The public marketing reference to 35 or 30 ECTS does not override the adopted 30-EC EA2030 norm. The journey diagram confirms the block/project order; its project-4 label Management is descriptive, while the OER label Organisation controls. No clinical licence or medical-master admission is inferred for UCR.

components.name: Year 1 integrated medical curriculum
components.note: Workload accounting group: five case-based blocks (healthy start; growth/development I and II; infection/immunity; internal/external threats), Medical Science and Sustainable Public Health projects, and all five integrated longitudinal lines. This is not a separately awarded 60-EC course.

components.name: Year 2 integrated medical curriculum
components.note: Workload accounting group: Homeostasis I and II, Regulation, Reproduction/Gynaecology, Food Intake/Processing, Health & Technology and Care Policy & Organisation projects, and the five integrated longitudinal lines. This is not a separately awarded 60-EC course.

components.name: Broadening minor
components.note: A 30-EC broadening minor completed in the first half of year 3 under the programme's minor rules.

components.name: Year 3 integrated medical curriculum
components.note: Remaining workload accounting group after the 30-EC minor and separately specified 1-EC professionalism requirement: posture/movement, brain/senses, ageing/end of life, integrated lines and competency-linked final works. No individual block EC is inferred.

components.name: Longitudinal professionalism
components.note: The programme separately awards 1 EC at the final examination when longitudinal professional conduct is sufficient.

alternatives.concept: This biomedical programme studies normal body structure and function, cellular and biochemical processes, pathology, immunity, pharmacology, brain and behaviour, health psychology, epidemiology and research. Its substantial health-science content responds to the scientific foundations of Medicine. It does not reproduce Erasmus’s integrated clinical reasoning, patient interviewing, physical examination, supervised care or professional formation, and it does not qualify a student to practise medicine.

alternatives.labelRationale: The route combines the strongest available UCR biomedical, life-science, neuroscience, psychology, public-health and research-methods sequence. The label names those available academic fields and deliberately does not imply clinical medical training or a qualifying Medicine degree.

alternatives.concept: A health-technology programme connects physiology, disease mechanisms, pathology, pharmacology, cognition and evidence synthesis with programming, mathematics, data management, machine learning, medical image analysis, deep learning, robotics and AI ethics. Some courses directly study medical applications; other computing and mathematical courses provide the methods needed to understand the technologies. It is an academic technology direction rather than training to deliver clinical care.

alternatives.labelRationale: The route retains a substantial biomedical and behavioural core while adding programming, mathematics, data science, machine learning, medical imaging, neural networks, robotics, databases and AI ethics. The label states this interdisciplinary direction without claiming a dedicated biomedical-engineering or clinical-technology degree.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: Compared with the closest match, this route removes dedicated epidemiology, anatomy, molecular cell biology, biochemistry, infection and immunity, neurobiology, abnormal psychology, medical and health psychology, sociology, psychodiagnostics and lifespan psychology. It adds programming, mathematical methods, introductory and advanced data science, machine learning, computer vision, databases, algorithms, linear algebra, robotics and AI ethics. Thirteen courses are shared and eleven differ, shifting the organising logic from broad biomedical and behavioural study to computation and emerging healthcare technology.

alternatives.concept: A population-health programme combines epidemiology, infection, disease mechanisms, physiology and pharmacology with health psychology, lifespan development, statistics and evidence synthesis. Social psychology, sociology, ethics, public and behavioural economics, qualitative methods, organisational psychology and scientific communication support the study of prevention, unequal health and healthcare organisation. The policy and organisational courses supply general analytical tools; they are not specialist health-policy or clinical training.

alternatives.labelRationale: The corrected curriculum has a substantial health-science base plus epidemiology, health psychology and research, complemented by social, economic and organisational analysis. The label does not imply specialist healthcare-management teaching or clinical qualification.
alternatives.distinctnessRationale: The population-health programme shares 17 courses with the closest biomedical option and nine with the technology option. Relative to the closest option, it replaces anatomy, cellular/molecular pathology laboratory work and the neuroscience sequence with social psychology, qualitative research, ethics, public and behavioural economics, organisational psychology and scientific argumentation. These seven changes (52.5 EC in each programme) follow the shift to prevention, populations and the social organisation of health. The substantial biomedical and health-psychology base remains, rather than relying on generic social theory to supply health content.

progressionAssessment.rationale: The first semester establishes biomedical, behavioural, epidemiological and professional foundations. Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine precedes every selected life-science and biomedical course that formally requires it; Introduction to Brain & Behavior precedes all selected advanced cognition and psychology courses that require it. Research Methods & Statistics and the laboratory course precede the advanced statistical and evidence-synthesis work conceptually. The final four semesters progress through normal structure and function into pathology, immunity, treatment, higher cognition, health psychology, psychodiagnostics and advanced research. Every course is available in its assigned term and every formal prerequisite is completed in an earlier semester.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest option substantively owns biomedical foundations, illness experience/lifespan, ethical issues in biomedical research and scientific inquiry. The patient-facing clinical-practice cluster is explicitly rejected as a UCR direction: the current courses do not sustain medical interviewing, physical examinations, clinical case management or supervised patient care. Those interests are not claimed as fulfilled by general rhetoric or health psychology. This does not invalidate the strongest academic biomedical response: 21 of its courses are in health, cognition and behavioural science, with statistics and social analysis supporting them. The evidence-backed technology direction retains a substantial biomedical base and adds computational methods, imaging and responsible AI. The population-health direction has been repaired to combine health science and prevention with population, behavioural and organisational analysis. All three pass substantive and numerical distinctness: they differ by 11, 7 and 15 courses in the respective pairs. Three is the maximum reached after these checks, not a preset target; the clinical-practice candidate remains rejected.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both provide an integrated foundation in normal human biology, health and disease; the comparator additionally embeds clinical skills, professional identity and broader medical blocks across the full year.
Human Physiology directly supports the comparator's second-year emphasis on homeostasis and regulation, but represents only one scientific part of its integrated clinical year.

Both study health and human functioning across later life, ageing and the final phase of life; the UCR course covers the whole lifespan and is not a substitute for the comparator's integrated clinical block.
The comparator reserves 30 EC for an approved broadening minor. UCR flexibility is distributed across the full 180-EC curriculum, so no single scheduled UCR course is asserted as an equivalent minor.

Both develop ethical reflection, feedback, responsibility and professional identity longitudinally; UCR addresses these across a first-year personal and professional development course rather than clinical conduct across a medical degree.

notes.text: Erasmus combines biomedical science with clinical reasoning, patient interviews, physical examination, treatment planning, clinical skills and professional formation. The UCR programmes offer substantial related scientific study, with different emphases on biomedicine, technology or population health. They do not reproduce this continuous clinical curriculum or supervised patient care and do not qualify students to practise medicine. Admission to any subsequent medical programme requires a separate assessment.

audience.programmeDescription: Medicine at Erasmus University Rotterdam combines biomedical science with clinical reasoning, patient-centred skills, research and professional development. The curriculum follows health and illness across the lifespan and includes projects in medical science, sustainable public health, technology and healthcare organisation.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options offer related scientific study of health and disease, with different emphases on biomedicine, health technology and population health. They do not provide the integrated clinical training in patient interviews, physical examination and treatment planning that forms part of Medicine. They do not qualify students to practise medicine or guarantee admission to a medical master.
